analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax and generation-skipping transfer tax on large inherited estates.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill drew 172 cosponsors but never received a committee vote or any floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would permanently eliminate the federal estate tax — the tax on transfers of wealth at death — and the generation-skipping transfer tax, which applies when wealth jumps a generation, such as from a grandparent to a grandchild. Under current law, only estates worth more than roughly $13 million per person (about $27 million per couple) owe the tax, and it falls on the portion above that. Repealing it would mean heirs of the largest fortunes never pay federal tax on inherited wealth. The bill would keep a separate gift tax on transfers between living people, with a $10 million lifetime exemption.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates — those exceeding the current exemption of roughly $13.6 million per person — would inherit that wealth free of federal estate tax. Because very few estates owe the tax at all, the benefit would go overwhelmingly to families with the largest fortunes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Heirs of the largest family fortunes

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the estate tax entirely for deaths on or after enactment, so heirs of taxable estates would owe nothing on inherited wealth above the exemption.

Repeals the generation-skipping transfer tax, which currently applies when wealth passes to a grandchild or another person two or more generations below the giver, letting large dynastic wealth skip a generation of tax.
Keeps a gift tax on transfers between living people but lowers the rate schedule's top rate to 35% and sets a $10 million lifetime exemption, making it cheaper to give large sums away during life.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would lose the revenue the estate tax raises — a tax paid almost exclusively by the estates of the wealthiest few percent of decedents — leaving either larger deficits or the need to raise other taxes or cut other spending.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes removes the only federal tax that applies to wealth passed between generations above the exemption, shifting the burden of funding the government away from the largest inheritances.
The bill does not replace the lost revenue, so the cost would fall on the general Treasury — meaning other taxpayers through future taxes, or other programs through cuts, or larger deficits.
The accompanying gift tax changes would cut the top rate on very large lifetime gifts from 40% to 35%, a further benefit concentrated among people able to give away millions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain would be concentrated: only a small share of estates owe any estate tax, so repeal would chiefly benefit heirs of the largest fortunes. The cost — lost federal revenue in the tens of billions per year under current law — would be spread across all federal taxpayers. Supporters' common argument is that the tax forces family farms and small businesses to sell to pay the bill; but with exemptions near $27 million per couple, only a small number of such operations are actually taxable, while the largest estates get the largest benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2024 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Randy Feenstra introduced the bill on January 18, 2024, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
172 members cosponsored the bill — 170 of the 224 House Republicans and 2 of the 216 House Democrats.
The Ways and Means Committee never reported the bill, and it received no floor vote; the action history shows no steps beyond introduction and referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The general Treasury and federal taxpayers kept the estate tax's revenue, since the tax was not repealed; the bill's failure means heirs of the very largest estates did not receive a tax-free inheritance. The bill's supporters did not get a vote on it either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal Treasury and ordinary taxpayers

for.name: Randy Feenstra
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes on January 18, 2024.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: The committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never marked up or voted on the bill; it stayed at the referral stage until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Republican: 170 of the 224 House Republicans cosponsored, versus 2 of the 216 House Democrats.

industries.industry: Heirs of very large estates (wealthiest households)
industries.note: Repeal would let inheritances above roughly $13.6 million per person pass free of federal tax, a benefit worth the most to the largest fortunes. The lost revenue would otherwise be available to the general Treasury.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth advisory industry
industries.note: Estate and generation-skipping tax rules are the core of a large advisory business built around planning around the tax; repeal would shrink that market. This is a secondary effect of a bill whose main stakes are the tax itself.

industries.industry: Family farms and small business owners
industries.note: Supporters cite farms and closely held businesses facing the tax, and repeal would remove that exposure. Under current exemption levels only a small share of estates are actually taxable, so the bulk of the benefit would go to the very largest fortunes.
